paragraphs: “What Æsop?” the President asked sternly again.
“Oh, Pierrot ... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
Again and again the President warned Mitya, very sternly and with great force, to be more careful in his language.
“You are hurting yourself in the opinion of your judges.”

The counsel for the defense was just as clever in handling the evidence of Rakitin. I may say that Rakitin was one of the leading witnesses, and one to whom the prosecutor attached great importance. It turned out that he knew everything. His knowledge was amazing. He had been everywhere, seen everything, talked to everybody, and knew every detail of the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch and all the Karamazovs. Of the envelope, it is true, he had heard only from Mitya himself. But he described Mitya’s exploits at the “Metropolis” in minute detail, with all his compromising doings and sayings, and he told the story of Captain Snegiryov’s “wisp of tow.” But even Rakitin could say nothing definite about Mitya’s inheritance, and kept to contemptuous generalities.

“Who could tell which of them was to blame, and which owed the other money, with their crazy Karamazov way of muddling things so that no one could make head or tail of it?” He blamed the tragic crime on habits that had become ingrained over ages of serfdom and on the sorry condition of Russia, which came from the lack of proper institutions. He was, in fact, given some freedom to speak his mind. This was the first occasion on which Rakitin showed what he could do and drew attention to himself. The prosecutor knew that the witness was preparing a magazine article on the case. Later, in his speech, as we shall see, he quoted some ideas from the article, which showed that he had seen it already. The picture the witness drew was a gloomy and sinister one, and it greatly strengthened the case for the prosecution. Altogether, Rakitin’s talk fascinated the public with its independence and the remarkable nobility of its ideas. There were even two or three outbursts of applause when he spoke of serfdom and the sorry condition of Russia.

But Rakitin, in his youthful ardor, made a slight blunder, and the counsel for the defense promptly and skillfully took advantage of it. He was answering some questions about Grushenka. Carried away by the loftiness of his own feelings and by his success, of which he was, of course, aware, he went so far as to speak rather contemptuously of Agrafena Alexandrovna as “the kept mistress of Samsonov.” Afterward he would have given a great deal to take back his words, for Fetyukovitch caught him out over it at once. And it was all because Rakitin had not counted on the lawyer having been able to learn every detail so thoroughly in so short a time.

“Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the most friendly and even respectful smile, “you are, of course, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, I have just read with such pleasure? It was published by the diocesan authorities, it is full of deep and religious reflections, and it opens with an excellent and devout dedication to the bishop.”
“I did not write it for publication ... it was published afterward,” muttered Rakitin, for some reason fearfully thrown off balance and almost ashamed.

“Oh, that’s excellent! A thinker like you can, and indeed ought to, take the widest view of every social question. Your most instructive pamphlet has been widely circulated thanks to the bishop’s patronage, and has been of real service.... But this is the main thing I should like to learn from you. You stated just now that you were very well acquainted with Madame Svyetlov.” (It should be noted that Grushenka’s surname was Svyetlov. I heard it for the first time that day, during the trial.)
“I can’t answer for all my acquaintances.... I am a young man ... and who can be responsible for everyone he meets?” cried Rakitin, flushing all over.

“I understand, I quite understand,” cried Fetyukovitch, as though he, too, were embarrassed and in a hurry to excuse himself. “You, like anyone else, might well be interested in knowing a young and beautiful woman who would gladly entertain the _élite_ of the young men of the neighborhood. But ... I only wanted to know ... It has come to my knowledge that Madame Svyetlov was especially eager, a couple of months ago, to meet the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and promised you twenty-five roubles if you would bring him to her in his monastic dress. And that actually took place on the evening of the very day on which the terrible crime that is the subject of the present investigation was committed. You brought Alexey Karamazov to Madame Svyetlov, and did you receive the twenty-five roubles from Madame Svyetlov as a reward? That’s what I wanted to hear from you.”
“It was a joke.... I don’t see what interest that can be to you.... I took it as a joke ... meaning to give it back later....”
“Then you did take— But you have not given it back yet ... or have you?”
“That’s of no consequence,” muttered Rakitin. “I refuse to answer such questions.... Of course I shall give it back.”

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch declared that he had no more questions for the witness. Mr. Rakitin left the witness box with his character not entirely free of stain. The effect of the lofty idealism of his speech was somewhat spoiled. Fetyukovitch’s expression, as he watched him walk away, seemed to suggest to the public, “This is a sample of the lofty-minded people who accuse him.” I remember that this incident, too, did not pass without an outburst from Mitya. He was enraged by the tone in which Rakitin had spoken of Grushenka, and he suddenly shouted “Bernard!” After Rakitin’s cross-examination, the President asked the prisoner if he had anything to say, and Mitya cried out loudly:
“Since I’ve been arrested, he has borrowed money from me! He is a contemptible Bernard and a opportunist, and he doesn’t believe in God. He took in the bishop!”

Mitya, of course, was called to order again for his reckless language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov’s evidence was a failure too, but for quite a different reason. He appeared in ragged, dirty clothes and muddy boots, and in spite of the watchfulness and expert eye of the police officers, he turned out to be hopelessly drunk. Asked about Mitya’s attack on him, he refused to answer.
“God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will make it up to me yonder.”
“Who told you not to tell? Who are you talking about?”
“Ilusha, my little son. ‘Father, father, how he insulted you!’ He said that by the stone. Now he is dying....”

The captain suddenly began sobbing and dropped to his knees in front of the President. He was hurried away amid the laughter of the public. The effect the prosecutor had prepared did not come off at all.

Fetyukovitch went on making the most of every opportunity, and amazed people more and more by his detailed knowledge of the case. Thus, for example, Trifon Borissovitch made a great impression, of course, and one very damaging to Mitya. He worked it out almost on his fingers that on his first visit to Mokroe, Mitya must have spent three thousand roubles, “or very little less. Just think what he squandered on those gypsy girls alone! And as for our lousy peasants, it wasn’t a case of throwing half a rouble into the street. He gave them presents of twenty-five roubles each, at the least. He didn’t give them less. And what a lot of money was simply stolen from him! And if anyone did steal, he didn’t leave a receipt. How could you catch the thief, when he was throwing his money away all the time? Our peasants are robbers, you know. They have no care for their souls. And the way he went on with the girls, our village girls! They’re set up for life since then, I tell you. They used to be poor.” He recalled, in fact, every item of expense and added it all up. So the theory that only fifteen hundred had been spent and the rest had been put aside in a little bag seemed unbelievable.
“I saw three thousand, as plain as day, in his hands. I saw it with my own eyes. I should think I know how to count money,” cried Trifon Borissovitch, doing his best to satisfy “his betters.”

When Fetyukovitch came to cross-examine him, he hardly tried to refute his evidence. He began asking him instead about an incident at the first carousal at Mokroe, a month before the arrest. Timofey and another peasant called Akim had picked up on the floor in the passage a hundred roubles that Mitya had dropped when he was drunk. They had given it to Trifon Borissovitch and had each received a rouble from him for doing so. “Well,” asked the lawyer, “did you give that hundred roubles back to Mr. Karamazov?” Trifon Borissovitch shuffled in vain.... After the peasants had been examined, he was forced to admit that the hundred roubles had been found. He only added that he had scrupulously returned it all to Dmitri Fyodorovitch “in perfect honesty, and it’s only because his honor was in liquor at the time that he wouldn’t remember it.” But he had denied the incident of the hundred roubles until the peasants were called to prove it, so his evidence about returning the money to Mitya was naturally regarded with great suspicion. And so one of the most dangerous witnesses brought forward by the prosecution was discredited again.

The same thing happened with the Poles. They took up a proud and independent attitude. They shouted loudly that they had both been in the service of the Crown, that “Pan Mitya” had offered them three thousand “to buy their honor,” and that they had seen a large sum of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch put a terrible number of Polish words into his sentences. He saw that this only raised his standing in the eyes of the President and the prosecutor, so he grew more and more pompous and ended by talking in Polish altogether. But Fetyukovitch caught them in his snares too. Trifon Borissovitch was called back and, in spite of his evasions, was forced to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had swapped in another pack of cards for the one he had supplied, and that Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated during the game. Kalganov confirmed this, and both Poles left the witness box with damaged reputations, amid laughter from the public.

Then exactly the same thing happened with almost all the most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to cast a slur on every one of them and to send them off with a certain mockery. The lawyers and experts were lost in admiration. They were only at a loss to see what good purpose it could serve, for everyone, I repeat, felt that the case for the prosecution could not be refuted, but was growing more and more tragically overwhelming. But from the confidence of the “great magician” they saw that he was serene, and they waited. They felt that “such a man” had not come from Petersburg for nothing, and that he was not a man to go home unsuccessful.
